The case originated in an application (no. 36110/97) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Four Turkish nationals, Mr Galip Yalman, Mr Bahattin Sarısoy, Mr Osman Çağlayan and Mr Yusuf Çamca (“the applicants”) alleged that their case, which commenced in 1989 and terminated in 1996, was not heard within a reasonable time as required by the Convention. The applicants were represented by Mr S. Esmer, a lawyer practising in Ankara. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Convention institutions.

In September 1980 the applicants were taken into police custody and were subsequently placed in detention on remand on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. In September 1988 the Erzincan Martial Law Court acquitted the applicants of the charges against them. In March, April and June 1989 the applicants brought individual actions before the Sinop Assize Court against the Treasury, pursuant to Law no. 466. They requested compensation for their unjustified detention. The applicants appealed, arguing that the amount of compensation awarded was not sufficient. On 30 May 1996 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicants’ appeal and upheld the judgment of the assize court.

The applicants, together with Dr Price’s wife, were sued by ‘K’, a former patient of Dr Price, in respect of property in Florida. The writ was issued on 12 February 1986. Before the action came to trial, the plaintiff was adjudicated bankrupt on 9 August 1989 and the trustee in bankruptcy continued the action. On the fourth day of trial, while K was being cross-examined, an adjournment was granted because K claimed to feel unwell. It emerged that no medical justification could be given for his continued non-attendance, but nonetheless he remained absent for the rest of the trial. The judge found that the transfer of the Florida property should be set aside on the ground that the defendants had not been able to rebut the presumption of undue influence created by the discrepancy.

It originated in an application (no. 18711/91) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 4 April 1991 by a British citizen. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations. The applicant, Mr Anthony Boner, is a British citizen born in 1960. He lives in Glasgow, Scotland. On 14 December 1989 three masked men, armed with a shotgun and a knife, carried out a robbery at a post office in Glen Village, Falkirk, Scotland, in the course of which they assaulted three post-office employees. Between 29 March and 10 April 1990 he stood trial in the High Court of Justiciary sitting in Edinburgh. The applicant received legal aid for the preparation of his defence. When Mrs G. was called to give evidence, the applicant’s counsel objected on the basis of her earlier presence in court. The trial judge adjourned the case and instructed prosecuting counsel to make further inquiries into the matter. The jury found the applicant guilty on all the charges. Taking account of his numerous previous convictions, the judge sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. The applicant, through his solicitor, lodged an intimation of intention to appeal against conviction. An application to extend legal aid to the appeal proceedings had been submitted in May 1990. Despite the advice of his solicitors and counsel, Mr Boner decided to proceed with the appeal. The applicant, who had no legal knowledge and had no assistance with his submissions, presented his own case on 24 January 1991 before the High Court of Justiciary. The Crown was represented by counsel. There is no indication in the record that the court required counsel for the Crown to address it. The court dismissed the first two grounds of appeal relating to Mrs G. and held that these were ill-founded and that the trial judge had approached the matter properly. It did however examine other points raised by the applicant, but reached “the clear conclusion that there was no miscarriage of justice in the case’. The appeal against conviction was unanimously dismissed. The case was heard at the High Court in London.

The Government informed the Court that they had not previously been aware of the applicant's attempted suicide, but had now considered the psychiatric report of 14 September 2009. The decision of the Swedish Court of Appeal was made in 1981. The decision was made on the basis that it was not necessary to make the tax payments. The case was decided in favour of the tax payer's right to a full refund. The judge ruled that the tax was not required to be paid, and that the decision was based on the fact that there was no obligation to pay the tax. The Supreme Court of Sweden ruled that there is no obligation for the taxman to pay any tax. This means that the case is not a legal question of whether or not the tax is owed, but of when the tax will be paid. It is possible to make a tax payment in the future, however, if there is a change in law, the decision can be appealed.

In 1982 the Swedish Parliament passed a bill to make it easier to file a tax claim. The bill was passed in 1982 with the help of the Swedish Court of Appeal. In 1983 the Supreme Court of Sweden ruled that the bill did not apply to the Swedish tax system. The decision means that the tax bill does not have to be paid until after the tax claim has been processed. The Swedish tax payer will pay the tax, even though the tax payment was never made. This means the taxman has no obligation to pay for the tax. The taxman is therefore free to make the tax call as he sees fit. The court of appeal will not make the decision until the case is heard by the full court.

In 1982 the Supreme Court ruled in favour of the Swedish Government's decision to levy a 20% surcharge on earnings over and above £200,000. The decision was overturned by the Court of Appeal in 1985. The ruling was upheld by the European Court of Human Rights. The Supreme Court of Justice ruled that the rule did not apply to the Swedish government. The court also ruled that it was not obliged to comply with the rule of law. The Court of Appeals ruled in favor of the government’s decision to refuse to pay the tax. The case was appealed to the European court of human rights, which found that the charge was not a breach of the law. But the court also found that it would be illegal to charge a person for non-payment of a tax owed.

Ustawa o skardze na naruszenie prawa strony do rozpoznania sprawy w postępowaniu sądowym bez nieuzasadnionej zwłoki (“the 2004 Act’) entered into force on 17 September 2004. It lays down various legal means designed to counteract and/or redress the undue length of judicial proceedings. A party to pending proceedings may ask for the acceleration of those proceedings and/ or just satisfaction for their unreasonable length under section 2 read in conjunction with section 5(1) of the 2004 Act. The Supreme Court ruled that while the 2004 Law produced legal effects as from the date of entry into force (17 September 2004), its provisions applied retroactively to all proceedings in which delays had occurred before that date but only when they had not yet been remedied.

The applicant was born in 1943 and lives in Wrexham. She claimed that she was some GBP 24.04 per week worse off as a result of her transition from IB to the State pension. The applicant complained to the Department of Work and Pensions concerning the differential treatment but was informed that nothing could be done. The case was heard at the Supreme Court in London and the decision was returned to the Court of Appeal on February 11, 2013. The decision was made on the basis that the applicant had been given a fair hearing. The final judgment was returned on February 14, 2013, and the sentence was set out below.

The applicant was born in 1943 and lives in Wrexham. She was in receipt of long-term incapacity benefit. At age 60, which is the date of entitlement to the State pension for women, she ceased to be eligible for IB. In its place she became entitled to draw her state retirement pension which, based upon her contribution record, entitled her to GBP 57.81 per week (about 62% of the maximum rate) She continued to draw DLA. As a result, the applicant claimed that she was some GBP 24.04 per week worse off as a result of her transition from IB to State pension. She complained to the Department of Work and Pensions concerning the differential treatment but was informed that nothing could be done.

In August 2003 the applicant turned 60 years of age. Prior to that date she was in receipt of long-term incapacity benefit. At age 60 she ceased to be eligible for IB. In its place she became entitled to draw her state retirement pension. She continued to draw DLA. As a result, the applicant claimed that she was some GBP 24.04 per week worse off as a result of her transition from IB to the State pension. The applicant complained to the Department of Work and Pensions concerning the differential treatment but was informed that nothing could be done. The appeal was upheld by the Court of Appeal and the decision was upheld.

On 7 February 2008 the President of the Chamber decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was concerned that his attempts to confirm that he was receiving adequate treatment in hospital might be regarded by the prison medical officer as criticism. He expressed his concerns about his medical correspondence with his external medical specialist being read and applied to the prison governor for a direction that such correspondence should be accorded confidentiality. The prison governor subsequently reconsidered his decision after seeking advice from HM Prison Service Headquarters. On 20 February 2004 the presiding High Court judge, Mr Justice Collins, allowed the applicant's claim for judicial review. The Court of Appeal concluded that although the procedure set out in the prison governor’s letter of 28 November 2002 amounted to an interference with the applicant's right to respect for his correspondence, the interference was justified and proportionate. Lord Justice Sedley gave the judgment of the court. It was noted that there was no dispute that the reading of prisoners’ correspondence was governed by law, and that it was directed to the prevention of crime and the protection of the rights and freedoms of others. The Court of Appeal concluded that the monitoring of the applicant’s medical correspondence was a proportionate interference with his Article 8 rights. It did not exclude the possibility that in another case it might be disproportionate to refuse confidentiality to medical correspondence in the prison context. It was recognised that there was an inescapable risk of abuse, for example, if the applicant's prison life or treatment was made more difficult because of what he was observed to be writing. Petition for leave to appeal was refused by the House of Lords on the ground that the petition did not raise an arguable point of law of general public importance. The applicants were represented by Mr U. Isaksson, a lawyer practising in Stockholm, and by Ms S. Wikström, lawyers of the Stockholm Tenants' Association. In April 2004, the landlord initiated proceedings before the Rent Review Board (hyresnämnden) in Stockholm against the applicants and some other tenants who had installed satellite dishes in the same house. The landlord sought execution of the notice of termination, claiming that the applicants' satellite installation violated the express ban in Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. The applicants dismantled the satellite dish and installed a new device by placing on the kitchen floor an iron stand from which an arm was mounted. The Rent Review Board gave a decision on 21 October 2004 finding in their favour. The landlord appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt). The court held an oral hearing at which, inter alia, Mr Tornefelt gave evidence. It also made an inspection of the applicants' satellite installation. By a final decision of 20 December 2005, the court found that the applicants had disregarded their obligations. The court found that the applicants' dish was virtually always positioned outside the kitchen window and thus constituted a permanent installation. It concluded, contrary to the findings of the Rent Review Board, that its placement breached Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. Although their satellite installation did not pose any real safety threat, their interests could not be allowed to override the weighty and reasonable interest of the landlord that order and good custom be upheld.

The first applicant, Mr Abdisamad Adow Sufi, is a Somali national who was born in 1987 and is currently in detention in an Immigration Detention Centre in West Drayton. On 3 October 2003 he claimed asylum on the ground that as a member of the Reer-Hamar, a sub-clan of the minority Ahansi clan, he had been subjected to persecution by Hawiye militia. On 15 April 2005 the Secretary of State for the Home Department refused the first applicant’s asylum application, finding, inter alia, that the fact he had remained in Somalia until 2003 undermined his claim to be a minority clan. On 16 May 2005 he appealed against the refusal of the application on both asylum and human rights grounds, namely Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention. On 29 June 2005 both the asylum appeal and the human rights appeal were dismissed by an Adjudicator who found that his account of what had happened to him in Somalia was not credible. He was later sentenced to three months’ imprisonment following a conviction for indecent exposure in October 2007.

The applicant, seeking the annulment of the Government’s decision of 21 June 1989, applied to the Supreme Administrative Court (regeringsrätten) for review under the 1988 Act on Judicial Review of Certain Administrative Decisions. He alleged that, by denying him a special extraction permit, the competent authorities had prevented him from taking measures to comply with the restoration plan. The refusal contravened the principle of objectivity enshrined in Chapter 1, section 9, of the Instrument of Government. The Court held in a judgment of 18 February 1991 (Series A no. 192) that there had been a violation of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention.

An agricultural engineer, Anders Fredin, is a Swedish citizen. He lives at Grödinge, Sweden. The applicant and his wife own land in the municipality of Botkyrka, on which there is a gravel pit. They held a permit to extract gravel from the pit from 14 April 1983 until 1 December 1988, when the permit was revoked. The revocation of the permit, and the lack of a court remedy against this and a related measure, gave rise to an earlier case before the Court, which held in a judgment of 18 February 1991 (Series A no. 192) that there had been a violation of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention.

An agricultural engineer held a permit to extract gravel from the pit from 14 April 1983 until 1 December 1988, when the permit was revoked. The applicant applied to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) for a special extraction permit, so that he could comply with a plan adopted by the Board on 9 March 1987 for the restoration of the pit. The application was dismissed on 14 March 1989 and an appeal by the applicant against this decision was rejected by the Government (the Ministry of Environment and Energy) on 21 June 1989. The Court held in a judgment of 18 February 1991 (Series A no. 192) that there had been a violation of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention.

The applicant was born in 1950 and is currently serving a sentence of imprisonment in HM Prison Rye Hill, Warwickshire. He is barred by section 3 of the Representation of the People Act 1983 from voting in parliamentary or local elections. He issued proceedings in the High Court under section 4 of the Human Rights Act 1998, seeking a declaration that this provision was incompatible with the European Convention on Human Rights. In its judgment dated 4 April 2001, the Divisional Court noted that in Europe only eight countries, including the United Kingdom, did not give convicted prisoners a vote. The cases before the European Commission of Human Rights and this Court were also reviewed.

Convicted prisoners have forfeited their right to have a say in the way the country is governed. The Working Group said that such prisoners had lost the moral authority to vote. Parliament in this country could have provided differently in order to meet the objectives which it discerned. Like McLachlin J in Canada, I would accept that the tailoring process seldom admits of perfection, so the courts must afford some leeway to the legislator. That applies even to the ‘hard’ cases, such as that in the case of Mathieu-Mohin. The United Kingdom falls into the middle of the spectrum, but its position in the spectrum is plainly a matter for Parliament not for the courts.

Parliament has taken the view that for the period during which they are in custody convicted prisoners have forfeited their right to have a say in the way the country is governed. The Working Group said that such prisoners had lost the moral authority to vote. There is a broad spectrum of approaches among democratic societies, and the United Kingdom falls into the middle of the spectrum. In course of time this position may move, either by way of further fine tuning, as was recently done in relation to remand prisoners and others, or more radically. But its position in the spectrum is plainly a matter for Parliament not for the courts. That applies even to the ‘hard cases’.

Parliament has taken the view that for the period during which they are in custody convicted prisoners have forfeited their right to have a say in the way the country is governed. The Working Group said that such prisoners had lost the moral authority to vote. The European Court also requires that the means employed to restrict the implied Convention rights to vote are not disproportionate, and that is the point at which, as it seems to me, it is appropriate for this court to defer to the legislature. Parliament in this country could have provided differently in order to meet the objectives which it discerned, and like McLachlin J in Canada, I would accept that the tailoring process seldom admits of perfection.

The applicant, Mrs Anne-Marie Andersson was a Swedish citizen. She was born in 1943 and died in 1996 (see paragraph 6 above). She lived in Göteborg, where she worked as a taxi driver. From May 1988 onwards she was unable to work as a result both of dental problems which caused her severe pain and anxiety about a dispute with her landlord. In April 1989 she contacted a psychiatric clinic to receive a medical certificate which would enable her to claim sickness benefit from the Health Insurance Office. From 20 August 1991 the applicant was treated by the chief psychiatrist who drew her attention to the possible detrimental effect her situation might have on her son. In January 1992 the psychiatrist informed Mrs Andersson that since the child's health might be at risk, she had an obligation under Swedish law to contact the social authorities.

The applicant, Mrs Anne-Marie Andersson was a Swedish citizen. She was born in 1943 and died in 1996. She lived in Göteborg, where she worked as a taxi driver. At the time of the events in question, she was divorced and living with her youngest son. From May 1988 onwards she was unable to work as a result of dental problems which caused her severe pain and anxiety about a dispute with her landlord. In April 1989 she contacted a psychiatric clinic to receive a medical certificate which would enable her to claim sickness benefit from the Health Insurance Office. From 20 August 1991 the applicant was treated by the chief psychiatrist who drew her attention to the possible detrimental effect her situation might have on her son.

The psychiatrist's concern for the applicant's son was shared by the headmaster and a teacher at the school he attended. In October 1991 they had contacted the Social Council and expressed concern about his learning difficulties and his general state of health. Following this, the Council commenced an investigation which, with Mrs Andersson's agreement, led to the placement of her son in a non-residential therapeutic school on 2 March 1992. The application was denied on the basis that the boy was not mentally ill. The case was heard in front of the European Court of Human Rights. The judge ruled that the applicant should be allowed to stay at the therapeutic school.

background_knowledge: Case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant invoked Articles 6, 13 and 14 of the Convention. He alleged that the issue of a certificate emanating from the Secretary of State, under section 42 of the Fair Employment (Northern Ireland) Act 1976, operated under the terms of the 1976 Act. He also claimed that he had no effective remedy before a national authority in breach of Article 13, and that he has been discriminated against contrary to Article 14 in conjunction with Article 6. The application was declared admissible by the Commission on 24 February 1997 and transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1999 in accordance with Article 5 § 3, second sentence, of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention, the Commission not having completed its examination of the case by that date.

The applicant began work in the Culloden Hotel, Belfast, as a silver service waiter. He claims he was unlawfully discriminated against on the grounds of religious belief or political opinion. The Fair Employment Tribunal then of its own motion fixed a preliminary hearing for determination of the following issue: “Whether the tribunal has jurisdiction to consider the applicant’s complaint in view of the circumstances” The applicant believes that he was the only Catholic in the restaurant. The applicant and 13 of his fifteen siblings are not involved in any politically related activity. The case was decided by the tribunal on a majority of three-to-one vote. The judge ruled that the tribunal did not have jurisdiction to entertain the complaint.

rewrited_text: The case originated in an application (no. 24265/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant invoked Articles 6, 13 and 14 of the Convention. He alleged that the issue of a certificate emanating from the Secretary of State, under section 42 of the Fair Employment (Northern Ireland) Act 1976, operated under the terms of the 1976 Act to deny him access to a court or tribunal. The applicant began work in the Culloden Hotel, Belfast, as a silver service waiter in August 1992. On 31 October 1992, the restaurant manager informed the applicant that he was being dismissed forthwith. The applicant was given no reason whatsoever for his peremptory dismissal. He made a complaint to the Fair Employment Tribunal that he had been unlawfully discriminated against on the grounds of religious belief or political opinion. The matter first came before the Fair Employment Tribunal on 3 June 1994. The applicant stated that he did not know the basis upon which the certificate was issued. He had never been shown, and was not entitled to demand, sight of the information, if any, which was placed before the Secretary of State which led to the certificate being issued. In light of the certificate, the tribunal declared that the decision by Moyola Cellars Limited to terminate its contract of employment with the applicant was for the purpose of protecting public safety and public order. The Fair Employment Tribunal found that the Fair Employment Act did not apply to the termination of the applicant’s contract, nor to the decision summarily to terminate the contract. “There is nothing for this Tribunal to consider in relation to that act [of termination],” said the tribunal. The tribunal dismissed the applicant's complaints in. relation to his dismissal and the manner of his dismissal.

He also claimed that there had been insufficient evidence to establish that the assault had resulted in the victim’s permanent disfigurement. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations. The applicant, Mr Peter Maxwell, is a British citizen born in 1944. On 14 or 15 February 1990 two masked men broke into a private house, situated in Stevenston, Scotland. They assaulted the occupant causing him severe injury and permanent disfigurement. On 19 February 1990 Mr Maxwell was arrested together with another man. They were indicted on a charge of assault. Both held in custody until trial started on 28 May 1990 in the High Court of Justiciary at Kilmarnock. On 29 May 1990 the jury found the applicant guilty of the charge. Taking account of his bad criminal record, the judge sentenced him to five years' imprisonment. The applicant lodged with the court a note of appeal setting out grounds which he formulated himself. The grounds of appeal can be summarised as follows: (a) the applicant had not been able to substantiate his contention that a crucial witness was giving false evidence against him because to do so would have involved revealing to the jury a previous conviction; (b) a number of witnesses had not be called by the Crown or by the Defence; (c) crucial evidence had been entirely fabricated; (d) the verdict of the jury was not supported by the evidence. On 25 January 1991, the Board informed Mr Maxwell that his application had been refused as the Board was not satisfied, as it was required to be under the relevant legislation. His solicitors advised him that he should abandon his appeal but he chose not to accept their advice. The applicant decided to proceed with his appeal personally. The Crown was represented by counsel but there is no indication that he intervened at the hearing. On the same date the court dismissed the appeal.

In 1987 the applicants' daughter, C.Ç., was severely injured in an accident. On 24 November 1992 she underwent surgery at the Ege University Plastic Surgery Department to repair the damage to her scalp. Prior to the operation, the doctors informed the applicants about the risks involved. The applicants filed an action with the Izmir Civil Court of First Instance against the doctors who performed the operation and claimed compensation for medical malpractice.
